rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the “small” sin is laughter, given as an example; the rest of the verse is clear.
rows.anchor: «الصغيرة» الضحك، وهذا مثال، وباقي الآية بين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode rebukes unbelievers for choosing Iblis, their enemy, over the one who bestowed every blessing, small and great.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية مضمنها تقريع الكفرة وتوقيفهم على خطاياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Remember when We said” is understood; the repeated story prepares the event here for rebuke, while al-Baqara presents its beginnings.
rows.anchor: وتقدير الكلام: واذكر إذ قلنا وتكررت هذه العبارة حيث تكررت هذه القصة،

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group understands prostration literally: faces on the ground as worship of God and honor for Adam, like prayer toward the Kaʿba.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هو السجود المعروف، ووضع الوجه بالأرض، جعله الله تعالى من الملائكة عبادة له

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group takes it as a gesture toward earth, since Arabic can use prostration for utmost humility, which people may be commanded to show.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة بل كان إيماء منهم نحو الأرض، وذلك يسمى سجودا لأن السجود في كلام العرب

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The line about hills prostrating under hoofbeats supports the figurative sense of prostration as humility.
rows.anchor: ترى الأكم فيه سجدا للحوافر وهذا جائز أن يكلفه قوم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Stand for your chief” and Abu ʿUbayda kissing ʿUmar’s hand in Syria illustrate deference; Saʿid b. Mansur recorded the latter.
rows.anchor: فمنه قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم «قوموا إلى سيدكم» ، ومنه تقبيل أبي عبيدة بن الجراح

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group reads the exception as discontinuous: Iblis was a jinn, not an angel; jinn-demons came from fiery flame, angels from light.
rows.anchor: قالت فرقة هو استثناء منقطع، لأن إبليس ليس من الملائكة، بل هو من الجن، وهم الشياطين

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some in that group call Iblis the first jinn and their progenitor, as Adam is the first human.
rows.anchor: فقال بعضها إبليس من الجن، وهو أولهم، وبدءتهم، كآدم من الإنس

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Others say Iblis and his cohort were jinn, while current demons descend from him as humans descend from Noah; his rebuke shows he was commanded with angels.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة بل كان إبليس وقبيله جنا، لكن جميع الشياطين اليوم من ذريته، فهو كنوح في الإنس

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: A connected-exception view makes Iblis an angel created from fire and “jinn” a description of hidden beings, including angels and demons.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة إن الاستثناء متصل، وإبليس من قبيل الملائكة خلقوا من نار،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some posit an angelic class called jinn in the lowest heaven and earth, governed by Iblis; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he counted among angels by exercising their commands and mission.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض هذه الفرقة كان في الملائكة صنف يسمى الجن وكانوا في السماء الدنيا وفي الأرض،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fasaqa means to leave or emerge; dates, seeds, and mice emerge from coverings, fruits, or holes, with corruption implied.
rows.anchor: ومنه قال فسقت الرطبة إذا خرجت من قشرها، وفسقت النواة إذا خرجت عن الثمرة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s five destructive vermin are called fawasiq because they cause corruption.
rows.anchor: وقول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم «خمس فواسق يقتلن في الحرم إنما هن مفسدات»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “He rebelled from his Lord’s command” may mean departing from the command, disobeying after it (ʿan can mean after), or departing by God’s will, with “command” used for will.
rows.anchor: وقوله عن أمر ربه يحتمل أن يريد خرج عن أمر ربه إياه، أي فارقه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Iblis was once from the noblest class and ruled heaven and earth before disobedience changed his state.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس في قصص هذه الآية: كان إبليس من أشرف صنف، وكان له سلطان السماء

rows.speaker: بعض العلماء
rows.claim: Some scholars say an error-based sin leaves room for hope, as with Adam, but pride-based sin does not, as with Iblis.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض العلماء إذا كانت خطيئة المرء من الخطأ فلترجه، كآدم، وإذا كانت من الكبر، فلا ترجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis’s offspring are whispering demons who urge evil and falsehood; “they are your enemy” uses a singular collective noun.
rows.anchor: وقوله وذريته ظاهر اللفظ يقتضي الموسوسين من الشياطين الذين يأمرون بالمنكر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid lists offspring: Zalanbur (markets), Tabin (calamities), al-Aʿwar (usury), Miswat (baseless rumors), and Dasim (entry into a home without God’s name).
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري أن مجاهدا قال: ذرية إبليس الشيطان، وكان يعدهم: زلنبور صاحب الأسواق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya omits these names as unsupported by a sound chain; he knows only Muslim’s wudu-whispering demon Khinzab and al-Tirmidhi’s wudu demon al-Walahan.
rows.anchor: وهذا وما جانسه مما لم يأت به سند صحيح فلذلك اختصرته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A bad exchange means replacing allegiance to God with allegiance to Iblis and his descendants; this is injustice because it puts things in the wrong place.
rows.anchor: وقوله بئس للظالمين بدلا أي بدل ولاية لله عز وجل بولاية إبليس وذريته،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I did not make them witness creation” refers to unbelievers or people generally; it rebuts astrologers, natural philosophers, controlling physicians, and others speculating about creation.
rows.anchor: الضمير في أشهدتهم عائد على الكفار، وعلى الناس بالجملة، فتتضمن الآية الرد على طوائف

rows.speaker: عبد الحق الصقلي
rows.claim: Abu Muhammad says his father heard al-Mahdawi report that ʿAbd al-Haqq al-Siqilli used this interpretation; some theologians also mention it.
rows.anchor: قال: سمعت الفقيه أبا عبد الله محمد بن معاد المهدوي بالمهدية، يقول سمعت عبد الحق الصقلي يقول

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the pronoun refer to Iblis’s descendants and belittles them; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the broader interpretation is more beneficial.
rows.anchor: وقيل الضمير في أشهدتهم عائد على ذرية إبليس، فهذه الآية، على هذا تتضمن تحقيرهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iblis and his descendants are the primary target, with astrologers, soothsayers, and Arabs venerating jinn included because Iblis misled them all.
rows.anchor: إن الغرض المقصود أولا بالآية، هم إبليس وذريته، وبهذا الوجه يتجه الرد على الطوائف المذكورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Misleaders” applies to those groups and Iblis’s descendants; support is a metaphor for an assisting ally like a human arm. Several readers vary the vowels of ʿaḍad.
rows.anchor: فهم المراد الأول ب المضلين، وتندرج هذه الطوائف في معناهم، وقرأ الجمهور، «وما كنت»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scene is a threat: God tells polytheists to call for help from partners they claimed; “my partners” means according to their claim.
rows.anchor: وقوله ويوم يقول الآية وعيد، المعنى واذكر يوم،

rows.speaker: طلحة ويحيى والأعمش وحمزة
rows.claim: These readers say “We say” in the first-person plural; most say “He says,” with God addressing the polytheists.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة ويحيى والأعمش وحمزة «نقول» بنون العظمة، وقرأ الجمهور بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaʿm usually reports uncertain, often false speech, though at best it means reporting while leaving responsibility with the speaker, as in Sibawayh’s “al-Khalil reported.”
rows.anchor: وقوله شركائي أي على دعواكم أيها المشركون وقد بين هذا بقوله الذين زعمتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols’ failure to answer is most plainly literal, though it could be figurative: the polytheists’ recognition of idols’ impotence is like calling without response.
rows.anchor: ظاهره أن ذلك يقع حقيقة، ويحتمل أن يكون استعارة، كأن فكرة الكفار ونظرهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو وأنس بن مالك ومجاهد
rows.claim: These authorities say mawbiq is a valley in Hell flowing with blood and pus; Anas says it separates Hell’s people from believers.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله ابن عمرو وأنس بن مالك ومجاهد: هو واد في جهنم يجري بدم وصديد،

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan interprets mawbiq as enmity between them.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن موبقا معناه عداوة وبينهم على هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Meccans open the final yā in shirkāʾī; the majority use hamza, either fully articulated or softened.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير وأهل مكة «شركائي» بياء مفتوحة، وقرأ الجمهور: «شركائي» بهمزة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take “between them” as a location separating believers from unbelievers or polytheists from idols; Ibn ʿAbbas explains mawbiq as destruction, while a meeting place is weak.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس موبقا معناه مهلكا بمنزلة موضع وهو من قولك وبق الرجل وأوبقه غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest reading makes mawbiq a noun: their connection itself is destructive; “between them” can be the first object of “made.”
rows.anchor: والأظهر فيه أن يكون اسما، بمعنى جعلنا تواصلهم أمرا مهلكا لهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The criminals see and face the Fire, knowing they will enter it; “they supposed” need not mean certainty, but can describe verified knowledge before the event occurs.
rows.anchor: ثم أخبر عز وجل عن رؤية المجرمين النار، ومعاينتهم لها، ووقوع العلم لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects taking ẓann as full certainty; the wording better marks genuine expectation, as Duraid’s line illustrates.
rows.anchor: ولكن العبارة بالظن لا تجيء أبدا في موضع يقين تام قد قاله الحسن،

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads “they thought they would meet it”; Ibn Masʿud’s codex matches, and al-Dani reports ʿAlqama’s doubled-f reading malaffuha.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش «فظنوا أنهم ملاقوها» ، وكذلك في مصحف ابن مسعود،

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reports the Prophet saying an unbeliever sees Hell and expects to meet it from forty years’ travel away.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو سعيد الخدري أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال إن الكافر ليرى جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-maṣrif means a place or route of escape, from turning away from one thing to another; Abu Kabir’s poem illustrates it.
rows.anchor: و «المصرف» المعدل، والمرغ، ومنه قول أبي كبير الهذلي: [الكامل]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God varied warnings and hopes and explained matters through examples useful for guidance; despite this, people turn aside and dispute falsely.
rows.anchor: المعنى: ولقد خوفنا ورجينا وبالغنا في البيان، وهذا كله بتمثيل وتقريب للأذهان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Humankind” is generic; disputation is verbal contention, and humans are more contentious than any beings they might dispute with, including angels and jinn.
rows.anchor: وقوله الإنسان يريد الجنس، وروي أن سبب هذه الآية هو النضر بن الحارث،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports name al-Naḍr b. al-Harith or Ibn al-Zabʿari as the occasion; another says the Prophet woke ʿAli after night prayer and repeated the verse after ʿAli said his soul was in God’s hand; Ibn ʿAṭiyya applies it generally.
rows.anchor: وروي أن سبب هذه الآية هو النضر بن الحارث، وقيل ابن الزبعرى. وروي أن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse laments their condition: they did not deliberately refuse belief to bring punishment, but thought themselves right although their course led there.
rows.anchor: هذه آية: تأسف عليهم وتنبيه على فساد حالهم، لأن هذا المنع لم يكن بقصد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The people” are Muhammad’s disbelieving contemporaries who resisted his law; “guidance” is God’s law and its exposition.
rows.anchor: والناس يراد به كفار عصر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، الذين تولوا دفع الشريعة وتكذيبها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking forgiveness means asking forgiveness for past unbelief and other wrongdoing; the earlier nations’ precedent refers to punishments such as drowning, the cry, darkness, and wind.
rows.anchor: و «الاستغفار» هنا طلب المغفرة على فارط الذنب كفرا وغيره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative is unfamiliar punishment coming face to face; the distinction matters, and the warning came true at Badr.
rows.anchor: أو يأتيهم العذاب قبلا أي مقابلة عيانا، والمعنى عذابا غير المعهود،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid explains qubulan as coming suddenly.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: قبلا معناه فجأة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qu-bulan has readings with kasra qaf/fatha ba, both rounded, or rounded qaf/silent ba; it can mean face-to-face or kinds of punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وأبو عمرو وابن عامر ومجاهد وعيسى بن عمر «قبلا» بكسر القاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Messengers promise Paradise to believers and warn unbelievers of the Fire, not debate or demands for signs.
rows.anchor: والرسل لم نبعثهم ليجادلوا، ولا لتتمنى عليهم الاقتراحات، وإنما بعثناهم مبشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yudhiḍū means make vanish or disprove; al-dahḍ is mire in which one slips, illustrated by a poetic line in the next segment.
rows.anchor: و «يدحضوا» معناه يزهقوا، و «الدحض» الطين الذي يزهق فيه، ومنه قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: نجى اليشكري
rows.claim: The line uses dahḍ for mire that makes a camel slip, illustrating the lexical image behind “make the truth slip away.”
rows.anchor: وردت ونجى اليشكري نجاؤه ... وحاد كما حاد البعير عن الدحض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat includes Qurʾanic verses and signs appearing through the Prophet; “what they were warned of” means afterlife punishment, with its object omitted, and mockery includes old-tales claims.
rows.anchor: وقوله واتخذوا إلى آخر الآية توعيد، و «الآيات» تجمع آيات القرآن والعلامات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question establishes that none is more unjust than one who turns away after admonition and forgets grave sins.
rows.anchor: وقوله ومن أظلم استفهام بمعنى التقرير، وهذا من أفصح التقرير أن يوقف الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hands are assigned to sins because they acquire physical things, a metaphor extended to moral actions.
rows.anchor: ونسب السيئات إلى اليدين، من حيث كانت اليدان آلة التكسب في الأمور الجرمية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kinan is plural of kinnan, a covering; the heart-covering may be literal, which is possible, or metaphor for hearts hardened and kept from good.
rows.anchor: جعل على قلوبهم أكنة وهي جمع كنان، وهو كالغلاف الساتر واختلف الناس في هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heaviness in the ears is plainly metaphorical: unbelievers hear the call but are unaffected; blindness and muteness likewise are metaphors, while debate concerns heart descriptions.
rows.anchor: وأما «الوقر» في الآذان، فاستعارة بينة لأنا نحس الكفرة يسمعون الدعاء إلى الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They will never be guided” may be restricted to those decreed never to believe, or mean none of the addressed group will be guided collectively; many converts require one reading.
rows.anchor: وهذا يخرج على أحد تأويلين: أحدهما أن يكون هذا اللفظ العام يراد به الخاص،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s forgiveness and mercy toward believers entail delaying punishment for unbelievers; if seized for their deeds, they would be destroyed immediately, but the deadline has no escape.
rows.anchor: لما أخبر تعالى عن القوم الذين حتم بكفرهم، أنهم لا يهتدون أبدا، عقب ذلك بأنه للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group identifies the deadline as death, another as afterlife punishment, and al-Tabari as Badr.
rows.anchor: قالت فرقة هو أجل الموت، وقالت فرقة هو عذاب الآخرة، وقال الطبري هو يوم بدر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawʾil means refuge or escape, from waʾala (to be saved), as shown by poems from an unnamed poet and al-Aʿsha.
rows.anchor: و «الموئل» المنجى يقال: وأل الرجل يئل إذا نجا. ومنه قول الشاعر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destroyed towns recall ʿAd, Thamud, Midian, and others; “people of” is omitted, as the pronoun refers to their inhabitants.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله وتلك القرى حذف مضاف تقديره وتلك أهل القرى يدل على ذلك قوله أهلكناهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those towns” may be the subject, with “towns” as adjective and “We destroyed them” as predicate, or an object of an implied verb.
rows.anchor: وتلك ابتداء، والقرى صفته، وأهلكناهم خبر، ويصح أن يكون تلك منصوبا بفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For la-mahlikihim most read rounded mim/open lam; ʿAsim via Abu Bakr opens both, via Hafs opens mim and lowers lam; groups differ whether halaka is transitive.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لمهلكهم» بضم الميم وفتح اللام، من أهلك، ومفعل في مثل هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s story begins a new narrative, with “remember” or “recite” understood; this is Moses Ibn ʿImran because the Qurʾan names no other and would identify another.
rows.anchor: وقوله وإذ قال موسى الآية ابتداء قصة ليست من الكلام الأول، المعنى: اذكر واتل،

rows.speaker: نوف البكالي
rows.claim: Nawf al-Bikali says this was another Moses, son of Mishani or Manasi; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as incorrect and says Ibn ʿAbbas and others refuted it.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة منها نوف البكالي أنه ليس موسى بن عمران، وهو موسى بن مشنى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Moses is Ibn ʿImran, his attendant is Joshua son of Nun, from Ephraim son of Joseph son of Jacob; fataa means youth and is a courteous term for servant.
rows.anchor: فهو يوشع بن نون بن إفراييم بن يوسف بن يعقوب، وأما من قال هو موسى بن مشنى فليس الفتى يوشع بن نون،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet encouraged saying “my young man” rather than “my slave,” teaching humility; Joshua was said to be Moses’s sister’s son.
rows.anchor: «لا يقل أحدكم عبدي ولا أمتي وليقل فتاي وفتاتي» ، فهذا ندب إلى التواضع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Moses preached impressively, said he knew no one more learned, then God told him of Khidr and the fish’s location at the sea junction.
rows.anchor: أن موسى جلس يوما في مجلس لبني إسرائيل، وخطب فأبلغ، فقيل له هل تعلم أحدا أعلم منك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says he will keep traveling until the seas meet; abraḥ means “I will not cease,” as al-Farazdaq’s line illustrates.
rows.anchor: وقال لفتاه على جهة إمضاء العزيمة لا أبرح أسير، أي لا أزال،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports Ibn ʿAbbas’s account that Moses settled the Israelites in Egypt after taking it, preached, and sought Khidr; Ibn ʿAṭiyya doubts it since Moses apparently died in the wilderness before the conquest.
rows.anchor: وذكر الطبري عن ابن عباس: قال: لما ظهر موسى وقومه على مصر، أنزل قومه بمصر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story teaches traveling to seek knowledge and humility before a learned teacher.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه القصة من الفقه الرحلة في طلب العلم، والتواضع للعالم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read majmaʿ with both mims open; al-Dahhak lowers the second mim.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «مجمع» بفتح الميمين، وقرأ الضحاك «مجمع» بكسر الميم الثانية،

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada locate the junction where Persian and Roman seas meet; Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes the ocean branch near Tangier.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد وقتادة هو مجتمع بحر فارس وبحر الروم.

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy b. Kaʿb locates the junction in Africa; other reports place it in the ocean/Andalusia region and identify the town with the green island.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي بن كعب أنه قال مجمع البحرين بإفريقية، وهذا يقرب من الذي قبله،

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Some say the seas are salt and fresh water, placing Khidr at a river’s mouth; others allegorize them as Moses and Khidr, a weak view since reports describe actual seawater.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة مجمع البحرين يريد بحرا ملحا وبحرا عذبا، فعلى هذا إنما كان الخضر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ḥuquban with rounded qaf; al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, and ʿAsim use silent qaf. Durations reported range from one, seventy, or eighty years to indefinite eras or years pluralized from ḥuqba.
rows.anchor: واختلف القراء، فقرأ الحسن والأعمش وعاصم «حقبا» بسكون القاف، وقرأ الجمهور «حقبا» بضمه،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes “between them” to refer to the seas; another view refers to Moses and Khidr, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the seas.
rows.anchor: الضمير في قوله بينهما للبحرين، قاله مجاهد، وقيل هو لموسى والخضر، والأول أصوب،

rows.speaker: عبيد الله بن مسلم
rows.claim: ʿUbayd Allah b. Muslim reads majmaʿ with the second mim kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبيد الله بن مسلم «مجمع» بكسر الميم الثانية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only the attendant forgot the fish, specifically to tell Moses what he saw; it is attributed to both because the attendant carried their shared provision and responsibility.
rows.anchor: وقال نسيا وإنما كان النسيان من الفتى وحده، نسي أن يعلم موسى بما رأى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Joshua saw the fish leap from basket to sea while Moses slept; he waited until Moses awoke, then forgot to tell him and they traveled on.
rows.anchor: وروي في الحديث أن يوشع رأى الحوت قد حش من المكتل إلى البحر فرآه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sarab means passage; the majority and Prophetic report say water stayed open behind the fish like an arch, while Qatada says it became solid rock.
rows.anchor: و «السرب» : المسلك في جوف الأرض، فشبه به مسلك الحوت في الماء حين لم ينطبق الماء

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says the fish tunneled through land from basket to sea, then swam normally; he takes sarab as roaming freely, as in Q 13:10.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد إنما اتخذ سبيله سربا في البر حتى وصل إلى البحر ثم عام على العادة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some imagined a tunnel through earth and rock from basket to sea, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the apparent account has the fish’s passage in water.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الأمر أن السرب، إنما كان في الماء،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A strange al-Bukhari report says the fish revived when touched by a spring called the spring of life; another says its passage became a stone road to the island where Khidr was found.
rows.anchor: ومن غريب ما روي في البخاري عن ابن عباس من قصص هذه الآية أن الحوت إنما حيي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The island-path report conflicts with the apparent account and wording that the pair retraced their steps; Khidr was found on the shore.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الروايات والكتاب أنه إنما وجد الخضر في ضفة البحر، يدل على ذلك قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report places the fish’s disappearance at a large shore-stone; after traveling overnight and into the next day, Moses became hungry and asked for food.
rows.anchor: وروي في قوله فلما جاوزا أن موسى عليه السلام نزل عند صخرة عظيمة في ضفة البحر،

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الجوهري
rows.claim: Abu al-Fadl al-Jawhari says Moses needed no food during forty days of intimate converse with God but became hungry during part of a day traveling to meet a human.
rows.anchor: سمعت أبا الفضل الجوهري يقول في وعظه مشى موسى إلى المناجاة فبقي أربعين يوما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naṣab means fatigue and hardship; ʿAbd Allah b. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr reads nuṣuban with both consonants rounded.
rows.anchor: و «النصب» التعب والمشقة، وقرأ عبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير «نصبا» بضم النون والصاد،

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Al-Tabari reports a group identifying the rock with Syria beside Nahr al-Dhib.
rows.anchor: حكى الطبري عن فرقة أنها قالت الصخرة هي الشام عند نهر الذيب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joshua’s “I forgot the fish” means he forgot to tell Moses what happened; “to remember it” specifies the fish by apposition.
rows.anchor: وقوله نسيت الحوت يريد نسيت ذكر ما جرى فيه لك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi and another group report ansānihi forms; Ibn Kathir adds a connecting yā, while Ibn Masʿud’s codex says Satan made him forget to tell Moses.
rows.anchor: وأما الكسائي وحده «أنسانيه» ، وقرأت فرقة «أنسانيه» وقرأ ابن كثير في الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sea-route phrase may be Joshua’s remark or an exclamation after the report; either reading marvels at the dead fish reviving.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون من قول يوشع لموسى أي اتخذ الحوت سبيله عجبا للناس،

rows.speaker: أبو شجاع
rows.claim: Abu Shujaʿ says he saw the fish, describing a half-fish with one eye and an empty other half; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also describes its thin covering and spine.
rows.anchor: قال أبو شجاع في كتاب الطبري رأيته، أتيت به فإذا هو شقة حوت، وعين واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording could be God’s narration: Moses took the fish’s land route in amazement, or its route amazed people; Abu Haywa reads ittikhādh as a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون قوله واتخذ سبيله الآية إخبار من الله تعالى، وذلك على وجهين:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses recognizes the fish’s disappearance as their goal and says they should return, retracing their tracks to avoid missing the way.
rows.anchor: المعنى قال موسى لفتاه أمر الحوت وفقده هو الذي كنا نطلب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read nabghi with final yā; ʿAsim and others omit it, while al-Hasan keeps it connected but drops it at pause; qaṣṣ al-athar means tracing a hidden track.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «نبغي» بثبوت الياء، وقرأ عاصم وقوم «نبغ» دون ياء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servant is Khidr according to the majority and hadith; an uncredited view that he was someone else is rejected.
rows.anchor: و «العبد» هو الخضر في قول الجمهور بمقتضى الأحاديث، وخالف من لا يعتد بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most say Khidr was a prophet; some call him a righteous servant, but the verse supports prophethood because his inward actions required revelation.
rows.anchor: والخضر نبي عند الجمهور، وقيل هو عبد صالح غير نبي، والآية تشهد بنبوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report has Moses find Khidr lying under his garment; after greetings and questions, each describes knowledge God taught him that the other lacks.
rows.anchor: وروي في الحديث أن موسى عليه السلام وجد الخضر مسجى في ثوبه مستلقيا على الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr knew divinely revealed inner realities, not outward legal rulings; Moses knew law and judged by apparent words and actions.
rows.anchor: كان علم الخضر معرفة بواطن قد أوحيت إليه لا تعطي ظواهر الأحكام أفعاله بحسبها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says Khidr was named after sitting on dry vegetation that sprang green beneath him; “mercy” here means prophethood.
rows.anchor: وسمي الخضر خضرا لأنه جلس على فروة يابسة فاهتزت تحته خضراء، روي ذلك عن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Bukhari report says Moses claimed no one was more learned, then was directed to Khidr; al-Tabari gives another account where Moses asks who is most learned and is told to add others’ knowledge to his own.
rows.anchor: أن سبب هذه القصة أن موسى عليه السلام، قيل له تعلم أحدا أعلم منك، قال: لا،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read min ladunna with doubled nun; Abu ʿAmr lightens it and rounds dal, which Abu Hatim calls two dialects.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «من لدنا» بتشديد النون وقرأ أبو عمرو من «لدنا» بضم الدال وتخفيف النون،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s question is a gently phrased request that eases the request for instruction, like the Prophet’s request to be shown his ablution.
rows.anchor: هذه مخاطبة المستنزل المبالغ في حسن الأدب، المعنى: هل يتفق لك ويخف عليك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On one interpretation, “Can your Lord bring down a table?” is phrased similarly as a polite request.
rows.anchor: وعلى بعض التأويلات يجيء كذلك قوله هل يستطيع ربك أن ينزل علينا مائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rushdan is read rounded by Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, and ʿAsim, open by Abu ʿAmr; grammatically it is a second object of “teach” or circumstantial.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن كثير ونافع وعاصم «رشدا» بضم الراء والشين، وقرأ أبو عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr says Moses cannot endure actions that look wrong according to outward law, because he does not know their wisdom or how they are correct.
rows.anchor: لا تطيق أن تصبر على ما تراه من عملي، لأن الظواهر التي علمك لا تعطيه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses promises patience with God’s will; Khidr tells him to refrain from questions until Khidr begins explaining what he sees.
rows.anchor: وأمره بالإمساك عن السؤال والإكنان لما يراه حتى يبتدئه الخضر لشرح ما يجب شرحه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nafiʿ reads tasʾalni with open lam, doubled nun, and yā; Ibn ʿAmir omits yā, while the majority use silent lam and fixed yā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع فلا «تسألني» بفتح اللام، وتشديد النون وإثبات الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read khubran with silent ba; al-Aʿraj rounds it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «خبرا» بسكون الباء، وقرأ الأعرج «خبرا» بضمها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says they walked by the shore until a boat passed; its crew recognized Khidr and carried them without payment. “The boat” is generic.
rows.anchor: روي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنهما انطلقا ماشيين على سيف البحر حتى مرت بهما سفينة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr struck a peg into the boat’s side and pulled out two planks; this is what “he damaged it” describes.
rows.anchor: عمد الخضر إلى وتد فجعل يضرب في جنب السفينة حتى قلع به، فيما روي لوحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses spoke because the visible act seemed likely to drown everyone aboard; readings vary between “you drown” and “its people drown,” and Abu Rajaʾ doubles the r.
rows.anchor: غلبه ظاهر الأمر على الكلام حين رأى فعلا يؤدي إلى غرفة جميع من في السفينة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imran means a dreadful, momentous matter; Mujahid says objectionable, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya says “momentous” is more specific.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد «الإمر» المنكر. قال القاضي أبو محمد: والأمر أخص من المنكر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most say Moses forgot their agreement; Bukhari’s Prophetic report calls the first incident forgetfulness. Mujahid says first forgetfulness, second conditional, third deliberate, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as all conditional and deliberate action implausible.
rows.anchor: هذا قول الجمهور، وفي كتاب التفسير من صحيح البخاري أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy says Moses did not forget; Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains Moses thought the agreement prohibited questions, not a necessary objection to a terrible act, and used an indirect truthful excuse.
rows.anchor: وروى الطبري عن أبي بن كعب أنه قال: إن موسى عليه السلام لم ينس، ولكن قوله هذا من معاريض الكلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s wording gives an excuse without explicitly saying he forgot the covenant; it permits that interpretation while remaining truthful, though Ubayy himself reports the Prophet calling it forgetfulness.
rows.anchor: فجمع في هذا اللفظ بين العذر والصدق وما يخل بهذا القول إلا أن الذي قاله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tarhiqni means to burden or add difficulty to me.
rows.anchor: وترهقني معناه تكلفني وتضيف علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A story has a sparrow peck seawater; Khidr asks how much it took and compares their knowledge beside God’s to the peck beside the sea.
rows.anchor: نزل عصفور على جنب السفينة، فنقر في الماء نقرة، فقال الخضر لموسى،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “knowledge” means known things, the comparison seems to make God’s knowledge finite, which is impossible.
rows.anchor: وعندي أن الاعتراض باق لأن تناهي معلومات الله محال، إذ يتناهى العلم بتناهي المعلومات،

rows.speaker: بعض
rows.claim: A proposed reading compares Moses and Khidr’s learning with knowledge God gives scholars through Resurrection; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it good, except a report includes all creatures’ knowledge too.
rows.anchor: وقيل فرارا عن هذا الاعتراض، يحتمل أن يريد من علم الله الذي أعطاه العلماء قبلهما،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison is figurative: no sensible image better conveys smallness than a point beside a sea; Khidr was not calculating a precise ratio with God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: فلم يبق مع هذا إلا أن يكون التشبيه بتجوز، إذ لا يوجد في المحسوسات أقوى في القلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After leaving the boat, they passed boys at play; Khidr chose a handsome boy and killed him by pulling his head off, crushing him with a rock, or cutting his throat, according to reports.
rows.anchor: فمرا بغلمان يلعبون، فعمد الخضر إلى غلام حسن الهيئة وضيء، فاقتلع رأسه،

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says the boy was prepubescent, so Moses called him pure because he had not sinned; another says he was an adult youth, whom Arabs still call a boy, as in Layla al-Akhyaliyya’s line on al-Hajjaj.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الناس كان الغلام لم يبلغ الحلم، ولذلك قال موسى زكية أي لم تذنب،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the boy did wrong, swore he had not, and his parents backed his oath and protected him from pursuers.
rows.anchor: وفي الخبر أن هذا الغلام، كان يفسد في الأرض ويقسم لأبويه أنه ما فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read zākiya; al-Hasan, ʿAsim, and al-Jahdari read zakiyya. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the readings mean the same, despite attempts to distinguish them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس والأعرج وأبو جعفر ونافع والجمهور «زاكية» ، وقرأ الحسن وعاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Without a soul” implies the boy was grown: killing would be allowed if he killed another, while a child could not be killed either way.
rows.anchor: وقوله بغير نفس يقتضي أنه لو كان عن قتل نفس لم يكن به بأس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read nukran with silent kaf; Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Bakr from ʿAsim, Abu Jaʿfar, and Shayba round it; it means objectionable.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «نكرا» وقرأ ابن عامر وأبو بكر عن عاصم وأبو جعفر وشيبة

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says killing is more objectionable because the wrong is visible and complete, unlike the boat’s impending danger; another says the boat threatened many and was worse.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هذا قتل بين، وهناك مترقب ف نكرا أبلغ وقالت فرقة هذا قتل واحد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both descriptions fit: the boat’s imr is more terrifying because disaster was expected, while nukr marks wrongdoing more plainly because harm occurred.
rows.anchor: وعندي أنهما المعنيين، قوله إمرا [الكهف: 71] أفظع وأهول من حيث هو متوقع عظيم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I told you” adds rebuke and severity; “after that” refers to the next episode although it was implicit before.
rows.anchor: وقوله بعد هذا يريد بعدها القصة، فأعاد الضمير عليها وإن كانت لم يتقدم لها ذكر صريح،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read fa-la tuṣāḥibnī; ʿIsa and Yaʿqub read fa-la tuṣḥibnī; other variants include “do not accompany me with your knowledge.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «فلا تصاحبني» ورواها أبي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وقرأ عيسى ويعقوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You have reached an excuse from my side” means Moses gave adequate justification.
rows.anchor: وقوله قد بلغت من لدني عذرا أي قد أعذرت إلي، وبلغت إلى العذر من قبلي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story may underlie three-day periods for legal deadlines and waiting for reconciliation.
rows.anchor: ويشبه أن تكون هذه القصة أيضا أصلا للآجال في الأحكام التي هي ثلاثة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse notes that the Qurʾan’s division reaches the letter nun in nukran at its midpoint after the disjointed letters.
rows.anchor: ونصف القرآن بعد الحروف انتهى إلى النون من قوله نكرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ladunī readings vary: most double nun; Nafiʿ and ʿAsim lighten it; Abu Bakr has a further light form, and one variant Ibn Mujahid calls mistaken Abu ʿAli accepts by Arabic analogy.
rows.anchor: «لدني» بفتح اللام وضم الدال وشد النون. وهي «لدن» اتصلت بها نون الكناية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read ʿudhran; Abu ʿAmr and ʿIsa round the dal, and al-Dani reports Ubayy’s Prophetic ʿudhri with kasra and final yā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «عذرا» وقرأ أبو عمرو وعيسى «عذرا» بضم الدال، وحكى الداني أن أبي روى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed mercy on Moses and us; al-Bukhari reports him wishing Moses had waited so more of the story could be told.
rows.anchor: وفي البخاري عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: يرحم الله موسى لوددنا أنه صبر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God pointed out parallels in Moses’s past: a box cast into water, killing an Egyptian, and lifting a well-stone for Shuʿayb’s daughters without wages, yet he objected to Khidr.
rows.anchor: وذلك أنه لما أنكر أمر خرق السفينة، نودي يا موسى أين كان تدبيرك هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The refusal of food and hospitality demonstrates how little the world matters to God.
rows.anchor: وهذه عبرة مصرحة بهوان الدنيا على الله،

rows.speaker: محمد بن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin names al-Ubulla, the stingiest and most remote from heaven; others suggest Antioch, Barca, Andalusia’s island, or Abu Hawran near Azerbaijan.
rows.anchor: فقال محمد بن سيرين هي الأبلة. وهي أبخل قرية وأبعدها من السماء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Village identifications depend on where Moses’s journey occurred; God knows its true location.
rows.anchor: وهذا كله بحسب الخلاف في أي ناحية من الأرض كانت قصة موسى والله أعلم بحقيقة ذلك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read yuḍayyifūhumā with open dad and doubled ya; Abu Rajaʾ and others read lowered dad and silent ya. Dayf derives from inclining to a place, as idafa inclines one thing toward another; al-Aʿmash reads “they refused to feed them.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «يضيفوهما» بفتح الضاد وشد الياء، وقرأ أبو رجاء «يضيفوهما» ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall’s “desire” is metaphor: assigning living beings’ actions to inanimate objects imagines how a person there would act; poetry and sayings illustrate it.
rows.anchor: وقوله في الجدار يريد استعارة، وجميع الأفعال التي حقها أن تكون للحي الناطق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read yanqaḍḍ, “fall”; a Prophetic report and Ubayy’s reading round mim and lighten dad; ʿAli and ʿIkrima read yanāqiṣ, “split lengthwise”; Ibn Masʿud and al-Aʿmash read “about to fall.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «ينقض» أي يسقط، وقرأ النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم فيما روي عنه «أن ينقض»

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: One group says Khidr demolished and rebuilt the wall, supported by Ibn Masʿud’s codex and Moses’s wage remark; Saʿid b. Jubayr says Khidr smoothed it by hand and it stood.
rows.anchor: فقالت فرقة هدمه وقعد يبنيه، ووقع هذا في مصحف ابن مسعود،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report that Khidr made the wall stand by hand is closer to the actions of prophets; Moses’s wage suggestion means food to eat.
rows.anchor: وروي في هذا حديث وهو الأشبه بأفعال الأنبياء عليهم السلام فقال موسى للخضر:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read la-ttakhadhta; Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Masʿud, al-Hasan, and Qatada use the alternate form, with some assimilating consonants; a poem witnesses it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «لتخذت» وقرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو «لتخذت» وهي قراءة ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy b. Kaʿb’s codex reads, “If you wished, you would have been given payment for it.”
rows.anchor: وفي حرف أبي بن كعب: «لو شئت لأوتيت عليه أجرا» ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr ends the companionship under their agreement; asking was the mildest objection, while Moses’s wage remark implied disapproval and endorsed taking payment.
rows.anchor: واشترط الخضر، وأعطاه موسى أن لا يقع سؤال عن شيء، والسؤال أقل وجوه الاعتراضات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayn signifies accord between companions, metaphorically from containment; repeating “between me and you” adds emphasis.
rows.anchor: والبين الصلاح، الذي يكون بين المصطحبين ونحوهما، وذلك مستعار فيه من الظرفية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future marker in “I will inform you” separates the next explanation from the finished conversation; taʾwil here means outcome.
rows.anchor: والسين في قوله سأنبئك مفرقة بين المحاورتين والصحبتين، ومؤذنة بأن الأولى قد انقطعت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read miskin with light sin; one group says the owners were temporarily vulnerable traveling merchants, another says ten brothers, five disabled and unable to work the boat.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور «لمساكين» بتخفيف السين، جمع مسكين، واختلف في صفتهم،

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: With doubled sin, some interpret masakin as sailors named for holding the rudder or helping steer; another group says it means tanners of hides called musuk.
rows.anchor: وقرأت فرقة «لمساكين» بتشديد السين. واختلف في تأويل ذلك فقالت فرقة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ordinary reading is strongest: they were weak people deserving compassion; faqir and miskin both indicate severe need, with maskana adding exposure and begging.
rows.anchor: والأظهر في ذلك القراءة الأولى وأن معناها أن السفينة لقوم ضعفاء ينبغي أن يشفق لهم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some argue a miskin with basic livelihood is better off than a faqir; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says both words indicate severe need, while maskana adds exposure and begging.
rows.anchor: واحتج الناس بهذه الآية في أن المسكين الذي له البلغة من العيش كالسفينة لهؤلاء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s saying that the miskin is not the persistent petitioner and Q 2:273 distinguish exposed beggars from needy people who do not show themselves; God made two charity classes.
rows.anchor: فأما حديث النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الذي هو: «ليس المسكين بهذا الطواف» . فجعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret warāʾahum as “ahead”; Ibn Jubayr and Ibn ʿAbbas read “in front,” while ʿUthman reads “behind” and adds “sound.”
rows.anchor: وقوله وكان وراءهم ملك قال قوم معناه أمامهم، وقالوا وراء من الأضداد،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warāʾahum keeps its basic sense “behind,” here in time: the king’s seizure would come later in the sailors’ voyage.
rows.anchor: وقوله وراءهم هو عندي على بابه وذلك أن هذه الألفاظ إنما تجيء مراعا بها الزمن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier scriptures are “between the hands” and Hell “behind” temporally, while “prayer is ahead” is spatial; this usage resolves the directional puzzle.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى في التوراة والإنجيل إنها بين يدي القرآن، مطرد على ما قلنا في الزمن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qatada’s argument that warāʾahum means ahead because Hell is “in front” is unsound; al-Zajjaj calls it barbarous, though a king could literally be behind them on their return route.
rows.anchor: ووقع لقتادة في كتاب الطبري وكان وراءهم ملك قال قتادة أمامهم، ألا ترى أنه يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports naming the king Hudad b. Badad or al-Julanda are unsubstantiated; “every ship” means good, sound ships, not every vessel.
rows.anchor: وقيل اسم هذا الغاصب هدد بن بدد، وقيل اسمه الجلندا، وهذا كله غير ثابت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy’s age was disputed; a report says he was created disposed to disbelief, supporting that he was prepubescent, though it may describe him as an adult.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث: أن ذلك الغلام طبع يوم طبع كافرا، وهذا يؤيد ظاهره أنه كان غير بالغ،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy’s reported names, Jaysur with r or Jaysun with n, are unsubstantiated.
rows.anchor: وقيل اسم الغلام جيسور بالراء، وقيل جيسون بالنون، وهذا أمر كله غير ثابت،

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading adds that the boy was an unbeliever while his parents were believers.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي بن كعب: «فكان كافرا وكان أبواه مؤمنين» ،

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid reads “his parents were believers” with kāna construed impersonally, “it was the case that.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو سعيد الخدري «فكان أبواه مؤمنان» فجعلها كان التي فيها الأمر والشأن،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take “we feared” as Khidr speaking for himself and righteous companions; others make it God’s voice through Khidr. Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers a human-perspective metaphor despite the wording’s resistance; Ibn Masʿud makes it explicit.
rows.anchor: والضمير عندي للخضر وأصحابه الصالحين الذين أهمهم الأمر وتكلموا فيه،

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari glosses khashina as “We knew”; another says “We disliked.” Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares divine hope and fear language with laʿalla and ʿasa, framed by human listeners.
rows.anchor: قال الطبري معناه فعلمنا وقال غيره معناه فكرهنا والأظهر عندي في توجيه هذا التأويل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yurhiq means to overwhelm and burden the parents harshly: the boy’s love would make them follow him in rebellion and unbelief.
rows.anchor: ويرهقهما معناه يحثهما ويكلفهما بشدة، والمعنى أن يلقيهما حبه في اتباعه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read yubaddilahuma with open ba and doubled dal; Ibn Muhaysin, al-Hasan, and ʿAsim lighten it and make ba silent.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور «أن يبدلهما» بفتح الباء وشد الدال، وقرأ ابن محيصن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakat means noble character, dignity, and calmness containing goodness and intent; rahm means mercy, either God showing the parents mercy or they showing it to the child.
rows.anchor: و «الزكاة» : شرف الخلق، والوقار والسكينة المنطوية على خير ونية،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ruʾba’s line supports rahm as mercy shown to the parents or child.
rows.anchor: يا منزل الرحم على إدريسا ... ومنزل اللعن على إبليسا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAmir rounds the ha in rahman; others leave it silent, with variation from Abu ʿAmr. Ibn ʿAbbas reads “their Lord is purer than him.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر «رحما» بضم الحاء، وقرأ الباقون «رحما» بسكونها، واختلف عن أبي عمرو، وقرأ ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports the parents received a Muslim boy, and separately a girl; another report says the mother was pregnant with a Muslim boy when the first was killed.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن جريج أنهما بدلا غلاما مسلما، وروي عن ابن جريج أنهما بدلا جارية،

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqash says she bore seventy prophets, also attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas by al-Mahdawi; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as far-fetched because prophetic abundance is known among Israelites and she was not one.
rows.anchor: وحكى النقاش أنها ولدت هي وذريتها سبعين نبيا، وذكره المهدوي عن ابن عباس.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two boys were young because the verse calls them orphans; the Prophet said there is no orphan after puberty.
rows.anchor: هذان الغلامان صغيران، بقرينة وصفهما باليتم، وقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم «لا يتم بعد بلوغ» .
